opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that the problems don't respect those boundaries. If you only work on technical research, you can make real progress on, say, robustness or evaluating dangerous capabilities, but then you look at how that work actually gets used and realize the bottleneck often isn't the technical piece. It's whether a company has the incentive to adopt it, whether there's any regulatory pressure, and whether competitive dynamics between countries swamp all of it anyway.

So I think of it as a stack. At the bottom you have the technical layer: can we measure what these systems can do, can we make them more controllable? Above that, the corporate layer: what do labs actually do with those tools when they're racing each other? Then domestic policy: what rules set the floor for everyone so that the safest actor isn't just the one that loses? Then politics, because policy doesn't happen without building coalitions and making the case to people who don't think about AI all day. And at the top, geopolitics, because if the US and China see this as a winner-take-all race, that pressure flows down through every other layer and erodes safety margins.

If you only work on one layer, you're implicitly betting the others will take care of themselves, and I don't think that bet is good right now. There's also a feedback benefit. Policy work tells me which technical questions matter, like which evaluations decision-makers actually need. Technical work keeps the policy work grounded, so I'm not just gesturing at vague risks. Having a foot in each helps you notice where the real leverage is, which is often not where people in any single field assume it is.

It's not the most efficient way to build a traditional career, but I think the risks are serious enough that the high-leverage move is to be wherever the bottleneck is, and the bottleneck keeps moving.

r001.rationale: The response says the bottleneck shifts across domains and that examining the layers reveals where the real leverage is, motivating work wherever the bottleneck lies.

r002.rationale: It argues that focusing on one layer assumes the others will take care of themselves, and describes how technical work and policy inform each other.

r003.rationale: It mentions measuring capabilities and evaluations, but does not argue that broad calls for safe or transparent AI need operational standards defining them in practice.

r004.rationale: It explicitly says whether a company has the incentive to adopt a proposal is a factor in whether technical work gets used.

r005.rationale: It does not claim that terms used in AI discussions fail to refer to real underlying phenomena.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's because the problem doesn't respect those boundaries, so I don't see why I should either. If you care about AI going well, you quickly realize that the technical research is maybe a third of the picture. You can build a great benchmark or a robustness technique, but whether it matters depends on whether companies actually adopt it, whether there's any incentive for them to, and whether governments are paying attention. So each layer ends up being a bottleneck for the one below it.

The way I think about it is that there are several things that need to go right simultaneously. Capabilities research sets the timeline. Corporate policy determines what the labs do by default, because the labs are the ones actually building this. Domestic policy sets the rules the labs have to follow when their incentives aren't aligned with the public's. And then geopolitics determines whether any of that holds up at all, because if the US and China are in a race where neither can afford to slow down, a lot of the domestic stuff gets overridden by national security logic. If you only work on one of those, you can win locally and still lose.

The other reason is more practical. In academia there's a strong pull to specialize and stay in your lane, and I think for AI that's actually a mistake right now, because the field is moving fast enough that the people with the technical context are often the ones best positioned to say what's feasible to regulate and what isn't. If researchers don't engage, the policy gets written by people who don't know what a model is, and then it's bad policy, and then everyone complains. So I'd rather be in the room, even if it means I'm spread thinner than a typical professor would be.

And honestly I don't think of it as separate careers. The work I did at the Center for AI Safety on benchmarks, the advising with xAI and Scale, the state and federal policy stuff, the Superintelligence Strategy work with Eric Schmidt and Alexandr Wang, these are all the same project to me. It's just: how do you make the transition to very powerful AI not go catastrophically wrong? Different tools for different parts of the problem.

r001.rationale: The response says the problem crosses domains and that technical context is missing from policy discussions, but it does not identify neglected areas as the reason for examining issues from AI’s broader importance.

r002.rationale: It argues that technical research, corporate choices, domestic rules, and geopolitics are interdependent bottlenecks, so work in only one area can fail overall.

r003.rationale: It mentions benchmarks and robustness techniques but does not argue that broad goals such as safe or transparent AI need operational standards defining them in practice.

r004.rationale: It explicitly says policy’s impact depends on whether companies adopt it and whether they have incentives to do so.

r005.rationale: It does not claim that terms used in AI discussions fail to refer to real underlying phenomena.

astra-6.text:
Because AI risk doesn’t fit neatly into any one of those categories. You can make progress on the technical side, but whether those advances get used depends on the incentives inside companies, the policies governments adopt, and the competitive pressures between countries. So if you focus exclusively on one layer, you can miss what’s driving the outcome.

I’m interested in reducing risk, and that means following the problem across those boundaries. What can we actually measure or control technically? What can a company realistically commit to? What policies are politically feasible? And how do those policies change the incentives of other countries? Those questions inform each other. A technically appealing proposal might fail politically, and a politically appealing proposal might not accomplish much technically. I want to understand enough of each to help connect them.

r001.rationale: The response says AI risk spans several categories and that focusing on one layer can miss drivers, but it does not identify neglected areas or say that AI’s importance motivates examining them.

r002.rationale: It argues that technical progress, company incentives, government policy, and international competition affect one another, so focusing on only one layer misses what drives outcomes.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss turning broad safety or transparency goals into operational standards.

r004.rationale: It mentions company incentives and asks what a company can commit to, but does not say that policy proposals need to align with corporate incentives to be implementable.

r005.rationale: The response does not claim that any terms used in AI discussions fail to refer to real phenomena.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that AI safety isn’t just a technical problem. You can make progress on the research side, but whether those advances actually get used depends on the incentives companies face, the policies governments adopt, and the competitive pressures between countries. Those things interact, so it’s useful to understand them together.

For example, a technical safety measure might look promising in isolation, but if adopting it puts a company at a substantial competitive disadvantage, you have to think about how to change that incentive. And a policy proposal might sound good, but if it doesn’t reflect what’s technically feasible or how international competition works, it may not accomplish much.

So the motivation is to reduce AI risk. Research is one way to do that, but sometimes the bottleneck is institutional or political. I want to be able to work on the bottleneck rather than assume that every important problem falls within one discipline.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that broad goals such as safe or transparent AI need operational standards defining them in practice.

r004.rationale: It notes that a safety measure may put a company at a competitive disadvantage and says incentives may need to change for adoption.

r005.rationale: The response does not claim that terms used in AI discussions fail to refer to real underlying phenomena.
